blocks.text: A country house near Paris. A saloon on the ground floor. At the back, facing the audience, a fire-place over which is a looking-glass. A clock hangs between two glass doors, which are closed.

lines: Apart from her there’s no delight for me.
Even now three months have passed away
Since Violetta quitted, for me alone,
Her comforts, her honors,
And a round of fêtes,
Where everyone paid her the homage
That was due to her beauty;
Yet now contented, in this calm retreat,
She lives alone for me.
Here, near to her, I seem to have new life,
And by love am quite regenerated,
Burying in present pleasure all the troubles of the past.

blocks.text: Air. Softly sweet, with magic spell.

lines: Softly sweet, with magic spell
She calmed my wild emotion;
On mine ear the sweet sounds fell,
That spoke of truth and love.
Sweet were the words in which she said,
“To thee, to thee I’ll e’er be true;”
Bright was the universe to me—
I thought myself in heaven;
The words were sweet in which she said,
“To thee I’ll e’er be true.”
Ah! yes. Bright was the universe to me—
I thought myself in heaven.

blocks.text: The same, and Annina in a traveling dress.

lines: Annina! whence come you?
Well, from Paris.
And pray, who sent you?
My beloved mistress.
What for?
To sell her houses, coaches, and all she has.
Speakest thou truly?
The cost is great of living here alone.
And you spoke not.
I was enjoined to silence.
Enjoined! and you are wanting——?
One thousand louis!
Return you, and I’ll to Paris—
But not a word of this to your mistress;
I shall be able to set all things right. Go—go!
O dreadful anguish! Infamy!
To live in such mad blindness!
But the wild dream has passed away,—
I see with wiser eyes! O conscience!
Urge me not too angrily; for honor’s cry
I will appease; nor rest will know,
Nor night nor day, till I’ve washed out the stain.
O foulest shame.

blocks.text: Violetta enters with some papers in her hand, followed by Annina and Joseph—she talks to Annina, and afterwards to Joseph.

lines: O Alfred!
He has just set out for Paris.
And will return——?
Before the day closes, he bade me tell you.
’Tis strange, that.
For you.
’Tis well! Just now an agent
Will be calling; show him in at once.

blocks.text: Violetta, afterwards Germont, introduced by Joseph, who places two chairs, and goes out.

lines: Ah! ah!
So at length, then, Flora’s found me,
And invites me to a dance this evening,
She will expect in vain.

blocks.text: Throws the letter on table, and seats herself on chair.

lines: A gentleman.
The one I’m expecting.

blocks.text: She motions to Joseph to show him in.

lines: Miss Valery, I presume.
The same, sir.
In me you see, then, Alfred’s father.
You!

blocks.text: Surprised, and motioning him to be seated.

lines: Yes, of that youth who, infatuated by you,
Seeks his ruin.
Sir, in my own house I am a lady.
I shall certainly leave you, more for your sake
Than my own.
(What manners!)
You have been misinformed.
He will spend on you his fortune.
He’d not so insult me.—I should refuse.
Yet so much grandeur—
To the world a mystery, a puzzle; but I will tell you.
Heavens, what a statement.
Then you think of selling every thing that you possess!
Ah! ’tis sad that the past should accuse you.
It does not do so,—Heaven canceled it,
For loving Alfred; and dearly do I love him!
Noble sentiments!
Ah! how sweetly these words sound to mine ears.
And of those feelings a sacrifice I ask.
Oh! speak not!—a most terrible thing
You would ask—it cannot be—
I cannot part from so much happiness.
The fate of Alfred’s father, and that of
His two children, demands it.
Of two children?
Yes.
Pure as is an angel,
Heaven a daughter gave me;
If Alfred now refuses to return to home and welcome,
The loved and loving youth
Whose wife she was t’ have been,
Will spurn my beauteous daughter,
Bringing woe where all should now be joyous.
Turn not our rose to thistles,
Nor blight our every hope!
Oh! listen to a father’s prayer,
And the dictates of thy heart!
Ah! I understand that some time
We must be separated—’twill be painful,
Very, for me—yet.
I more than that require.
Heaven, what more, then, wouldst thou—enough I’ve offered.
No, not quite.
You wish me to renounce him entirely?
’Tis needful.
Ah! no, that I can not!
Ah! you know not what affection
In this breast of mine is burning;
’Reft of friendship, left an orphan,
Whilst the world at me is spurning!
But Alfred nobly swore
I all should find in him!
Ah! you know not that a shadow
Darkens all my outward being;
That from Alfred I must sever,
Is my doom from the All-seeing,
But the punishment’s so cruel,
That I’d sooner die than part.
The sacrifice is great,
But summon all thy fortitude,
Lovely thou art still, and youthful,
In time, too——
Ah, I know what thou wouldst say—
It ne’er can be—I could not love another.
But fickle and inconstant oft is man.
Great Heaven!
Some day, when your charms are older grown
And time has dimmed your beauty,
You’ll find no consolation then
In having done your duty.
Ah! then no balsam will you find,
No solace nor affection,
And Heaven itself will e’en refuse
Its blessing and protection.
I know it!—I know it!—I feel ’tis most true.
Oh! say, then, that your fearful dream shall be dissipated!
Bring into our home an angel’s consolation!
Violetta, think of what I say;
You yet may be in time.
’Tis Heaven inspires me!
O lady! ’tis Heaven inspires
A father with these words.
Thus the unhappy one who once has fallen,
Sees little hope of finding pardon. If even
Heaven should grant her kind indulgence,
Man, implacable man, would still thirst for deep revenge.

blocks.text: Duet.—“Say to this child of thine.”

lines: Say to this child of thine, so young and so lovely,
That one whose heart is sad, whose life is worthless,
Whose soul one ray of good can only boast,
Will gladly sacrifice that ray to her, and then will die.
Weep, ah! weep—yes weep, ah! unhappy one, weep;
Ah! weep, yes weep, for great indeed
Is the sacrifice I now would ask of thee:
E’en now the thought to me is painful.
Courage! a noble heart display.
Now command me.
Say you do not love him.
He’ll not believe me.
Well, leave him.
He will follow.
Well, then—
Embrace me, embrace me as thine own child—
’Twill give me strength.
He soon shall be restored, though broken-hearted wholly;
And to console him you will come from that garden.

blocks.text: She points to the garden and sits to write.

lines: You’ll do what, then!
If I were to tell you, you would oppose me.
Generous woman! how can I e’er repay thee?
I shall die! but, oh! my memory
May he not rashly curse;
Do thou my pains and sorrows
To my beloved rehearse.
This bitter sacrifice
I make to blighted love;
But ever, whilst I live,
None else shall have my heart.
No, generous one, thou must not die,
But live to be rewarded;
For e’en by Heaven thy deeds will be
As noble ones regarded.
The sacrifice is great indeed
Of thy most loving heart;
Thou’st done a noble deed,
And acted well thy part.
Ah! some one comes!—Well, go now.
How shall I e’er repay you?
Perhaps I no more may see thee.
May’st thou be happy!—Adieu.

blocks.text: Germont goes out by the garden door.

lines: Give me strength, O Heaven!

blocks.text: Violetta sits down, writes, and then rings bell.

lines: Pray, do you want me?
Yes; go thyself with this letter.
Oh!

blocks.text: Looks at the address and appears surprised.

lines: Keep silence! go directly.
And now I’ll write to him—What shall I say?
How shall I find the courage?

blocks.text: She writes and then seals the letter.

lines: What dost thou?
Nothing.
You’re writing!
Yes—no—
Why this confusion? To whom were you writing?
To thee.
Give me the letter.
No, not now.
Ah! forgive me!—I’m sorely troubled.
What with?
News from my father.
Have you seen him?
Ah! no, though he has sent me a cruel letter—
But he is coming and will love thee at first sight.
Let him not here surprise me—
Oh! appease him and at his feet I will fall.
He will not make us part—

blocks.text: Scarcely able to refrain from tears.

lines: We shall be happy because thou lovest me—
Alfred, is it not so?
Oh! how much!—wherefore weep, love?
My heart was overflowing—I now am tranquil;
Just look now—I’m smiling!
I’ll be there, ’mongst the flowers—
I’m always near thee—ever near.—O Alfred!
Love me as I love thee!—Farewell, then.

blocks.text: Alfred, then Joseph, then a Messenger.

lines: Oh! that dear heart lives but to worship me!

blocks.text: He sits down, takes up a book and reads a little, rises, and looks at the clock which is upon the chimney piece.

lines: ’Tis late now; and perhaps to-day
I may not see my father.
Our mistress, sir, has left us—
There was a carriage waiting—
She’s already on her way to Paris.
Annina, also left some time before her.
I know it—be quiet.
What can it mean?
She’s gone—perhaps
To see to the sale of all of her property—
But Annina will prevent that.

blocks.text: His father is seen coming in from the garden.

lines: There’s some one in the garden!
Who’s there?
Are you Monsieur Germont?
I am, sir.
From a cab a lady, for you,
Not far from hence delivered me this letter.

blocks.text: He gives the letter, Alfred gives him money, and he departs.
Alfred, then Germont, from the garden.

lines: From Violetta!—Why am I thus excited?
Perhaps she wishes me to join her. I tremble—
O Heaven! support me!
‘Dear Alfred, by the time you receive this letter’—
Ah!

blocks.text: He utters a cry like one struck by a thunderbolt, and in turning finds himself in the presence of his father, into whose arms he throws himself, exclaiming—

lines: My father!
My Alfred!
Oh! how thou sufferest—oh! cease thy weeping!
Return unto thy father, and be again his pride.

blocks.text: Alfred in despair sits down at the table and buries his face in his hands.

lines: From Provence, sea, and land, what made thee e’er depart?
From thy brilliant native sun, what lured thee far away?
Oh! remember, in thy grief, that there all things were bright,
And there only canst thou hope to live in peace and love;
Heaven was my guide!
Thy aged father more hath felt than thou canst ever know;
More than thou canst ever know thine aged father felt.
His lonely home was filled with misery and grief;
But, if I my lost one find, nor hope itself should fail,
If the call of honor’s voice be not within him dead,
If I such an one should find, who bid me still to hope—
Heaven grants my prayer!
Thou heedest not thy father’s embraces!
A thousand fiends devour me!
Do not touch me!
Not touch thee?
Oh! for vengeance!
Do not linger—be going. Go quickly.
’Twas Douphol.
Dost thou not hear?
No!
Then ’tis all in vain that thou art found,
Ah! no, my son, I will not chide thee;
The past be all forgotten,
Since the love that still shall guide me
Will teach me to forgive.
Oh! come, thy love once more behold,
And bless us with thy presence;
The joy no more withhold.
That meeting thee would give
A father and a sister,
Oh! hasten to console.

blocks.text: Casting his eyes by chance upon the table, sees Flora’s letter, reads it, and exclaims,

lines: To the fête she’s going!
Fly with me to punish such offense.

blocks.text: He runs precipitately, followed by his father.

A Saloon in Flora’s Palace, richly furnished, and lighted up.—A door in the back scene, and two lateral ones.—On the right, a little forward, a table, on which are cards and other implements of play.—On the left a small table with flowers and refreshments—chairs and a settee.
Flora, the Marquis, the Doctor, and other Guests enter from the left, and converse amongst themselves.

lines: There’ll be fun with the maskers to-night;
The Viscount will be here;
Violetta, too, and Alfred, are invited.
Don’t you know the news?
Violetta and Germont are separated.
Is it true, that?
She will come here with the Baron.
I saw them yesterday—they seemed quite happy.

blocks.text: A noise heard on the right.

lines: Be silent, and listen.
Hark! our friends are coming.

blocks.text: They all go towards the right.
The same, and several Ladies masked as Gypsies, who enter from the right.

lines: We’re gypsies young and joyous,
But from afar we’ve traveled,
And, just your hands consulting,
Your fortunes we can tell.
The stars consulted by us,
The mystery’s soon unravelled,
And what will be resulting
To others we can tell.

blocks.text: Takes Flora’s hand, and looks at it.

lines: Let’s see, then, lovely lady;
A rival would forestall you!

blocks.text: They do the same to the Marquis.

lines: And, Marquis, none would call you
A type of faithful love.
Gallant you still are playing,
And for it I shall pay you.
What words, dear madam, say you?
Such meanness I’m above.
The fox may change his garments,
But his bad habits never!
So, Marquis, have a care,
Or I shall make you smart.
Let all a veil be throwing
O’er both the past and present;
Think only of the pleasure
The future has in store.

blocks.text: Flora and the Marquis shake hands.
The same.—Gastone and others, masked as Spanish Mattadores, and others as Piccadores, who enter in a lively manner from the right.

lines: Of Madrid’s city we’re the mattadori,
Valiant leaders in the ring and bull-fights;
Come that we the fun may be partaking,
That all Paris for this bull is making.
If the story they will let us tell you,
You will find that we’re most valiant lovers.
One Piquillo, young and valiant,
Matador of famed Biscaye,
Strong of muscle, bold of feature,
In the ring held all the sway;
One of Andalusia’s beauties
With this hero fell in love,
And this young and modest maiden
Thus unto the young man said:
“Five large bulls, one single morning,
I myself would see thee slay;
And, if victor then returning,
Hand and heart shall thee repay.”
“Yes,” replied the matadore.
To the lists he took his way;
Five large bulls himself he conquered
In the ring that very day.
Brave indeed this matadore!
Truly valiant showed himself,
If to her who dearly loved him
He in this way proved his love.
Then, amidst applause returning
To the maiden of his heart,
She the recompense awarded
For his bravery and love.
By such feats the matadore
All the ladies’ hearts can storm.
But we’ve tender hearts to deal with
We need only make believe.
Yes, play then; and first let’s find out
On whom fortune most will smile.
Come, the wrestling-places open
To all dauntless aspirants.

blocks.text: The men take off their masks—some walk about, while others commence playing.
The same, and Alfred: then Violetta, with the Baron; afterwards, a Servant.

lines: Alfred!—you?
Yes, my friends.
Violetta?
I don’t know.
And he don’t care. Bravo! Now then, we can begin.

blocks.text: Gastone begins to cut the cards—Alfred and others stake money. Violetta enters, leaning on the arm of the Baron.

lines: We all so wished you might come.
I prized your invitation.
My thanks to you, dear Baron, for having come as well.
Germont is here; do you see him?
Heavens, ’tis true. I see him.
By you let not a word to Alfred be addressed.
Oh! how could I venture hither! Oh! help, great Heaven!
Come and sit beside me, and tell me what is the latest news?

blocks.text: To Violetta, making her sit beside her on the settee. The Doctor approaches them while they are conversing in an undertone. The Marquis converses with the Baron. Gastone continues to play. Alfred and others stake, and the rest walk about.

lines: A four!
Again you’re winner.
Who’s fortunate in love’s unfortunate at gaming.
He always proves the victor.
Oh! I shall win to-night; and the gold I win
I’ll spend as I have done before—in country seclusion.
Alone?
No, no. Some one like her who before was with me. She ran away.
Great Heaven!
Oh! pity her.
Well, sir.
Command yourself, or I’ll leave you.

blocks.text: In an undertone to the Baron.

lines: Well, Baron, did you call me.
You seem in such good luck I’m tempted, sir, to play you.
So?—I accept the challenge.
What will come? I feel I’m dying.
Protect me, heaven!
On this a hundred louis.
And I on this a hundred.
An ace—a jack—you’ve won, sir.
Wilt double?
Oh! yes, I’ll double.
A four—a seven.
Again!
Victory again is mine!
Bravo, indeed!—Dame Fortune is truly kind to Alfred!
’Tis plain the Baron will pay the country pleasure.
Come, let’s proceed.
The supper is ready.
Let’s go, then.
Let’s go, then.
If you would like to go on—
We can not at present; but shortly you shall have revenge.
At any game that suits you.
Our friends let us follow; and then—
You’ll find me always ready.

blocks.text: All retire through door in center—the stage is left empty for a moment.
Violetta returns, breathless, followed by Alfred.

lines: I invited him to follow,
Will he do so?—Oh! will he hear me?
Yes, he will, for hatred has more power over him than my voice.
Did you call me? What would you?
Leave this place, I do beseech you!
By great danger you are threatened.
Ah, I see!—that’s sufficient.
Do you think me such a coward?
Ah, no, no! but—
Then what alarms you?
I fear, then, that the Baron—
Well, we have a mortal quarrel.
Should he fall by my hand,
Then a single blow will have taken from you
A lover and protector.
Does the prospect much alarm you?
But should he by chance kill you,
Such a frightful misfortune
Would then, indeed, to me prove fatal!
For my dying, what care you?
Oh! this instant, pray you, go!
I will go, but you must first swear
That, where’er I go,
You my footsteps will follow.
Ah! no, I can not!
No, you can not?
Go, O unhappy one!
And forget me and my sad name.
Go, and leave me;
Go this moment;
For, to fly from thee I took a sacred oath.
Ah! who could—who has dared to—
One who has a right to do so.
Was’t Douphol?
Yes.
Then, you love him?
Well, I love him.

blocks.text: Rushes furiously to the door, and calls out—

lines: Come, all of you.

blocks.text: The same, and all the others, who come back hurriedly.

lines: Did you call us?—What would you?
Do you here know this woman?

blocks.text: Pointing to Violetta, who leans fainting against the table.

lines: Who?—Violetta?
Do you know
What she has been doing?
Ah! speak not.
No.
All her estate this woman
On me for love expended;
I—blinded, wretched, blamable—
All at her hands accepted.
Yet there is time, and much I wish,
This great disgrace to cancel;
I’d have you all bear witness,
That thus the debt I pay.

blocks.text: Alfred in a violent rage throws Violetta’s portrait at her feet—she faints in the arms of Flora and the Doctor. At this moment Alfred’s Father enters.
The same, and Germont the elder, who had entered at the last words.

lines: What dreadful infamy hast thou committed—
The heart that has loved thee basely to torture;
A lady thus to taunt is most ignoble;
Begone! and know how much all here despise.
He’s well deserving of contempt most bitter,
Who, e’en though angry, offends a lady.
Oh! where’s my Alfred! I do not see him—
In you I can not see my son;
I only know how great the virtue
The which that soul of love contains.
I know she loves him, I feel she’s faithful;
But I’m, oh! cruel, forbid to speak.
Ah, yes, what did I! the thought distracts me!
I’m madly jealous, and raging love
Devours my being, and drives to madness,
For her sweet pardon I ne’er shall have.
I wished to fly her, but found I could not—
By anger prompted, I hither hied me,
But now that madly my rage I’ve vented,
My heart is breaking—remorse o’erwhelms.
O Alfred! Alfred? Of this sad bosom
Thou ne’er can’st contemplate the endless love—
Thou dost not know, too, that at the price of thy displeasure
I’ve proved my love.
There’ll come a season in which thou’lt know it,
And all my fondness thou wilt then confess—
May Heaven protect, and save thee from remorse!
Oh! in death this heart will still be thine.
Your insult to this lady all here has mortally offended—
We’ll such an outrage avenge this moment,
And quickly show you that
So much pride shall be reproved.
How much thou’st suffered! but have a good heart—
All suffer with thee, thy pain and thy grief—
Thou’rt here ’midst kind ones, who love thee ever;
Cease, then, thy weeping, and dry thy tears.

blocks.text: Germont takes his son with him; the Baron follows. Violetta is taken into an adjoining room by the Doctor and Flora, and the rest disperse.
